en: The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle One, totaling twenty-eight thousand verses, composed by the Venerable Sthiramati (translated into Chinese as An-hui).
Homage to the Blessed One, the mountain of manifold virtues; homage to the Dharma, the great ocean of wisdom.
I prostrate to the harmonious Saṃgha, To this master of the treatise and to my own teacher.
Like a firefly’s glow assisting the sunlight, I shall propagate the Abhidharma-piṭaka according to my strength;
For the benefit of all beings and so that the Dharma may endure long, May you protect and sustain me with your majestic spiritual power.

Chapter One: The Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga) The first chapter, "Analysis of the Elements," consists of seven topics: namely, perfection of knowledge, perfection of abandonment, perfection of benefiting others, perfection of skillful means, perfection of being worthy of offerings, perfection of the aspirational resolve, and perfection of application.

Because of reverence for the Dharma, one constantly delights in hearing it; because of hearing it, the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) arises; because of the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) arises; and because of initiating the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is produced.

Because untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is able to sever all afflictions, and because it serves as the cause for the severance of those afflictions, one immediately realizes cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore, this is called the benefit that is the objective.
Regarding the seven meanings, the verse states that "all types of darkness are extinguished," which refers to the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃpad*).
The cessation of all [defilements] is the perfection of abandonment.
To uproot sentient beings from the mire of birth and death is the perfection of benefiting others.
To pay homage to such a one is the perfection of being worthy of offerings (*arhat*).
"The Teacher who acts according to reality" refers to the perfection of skillful means (*upāya*),
because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses supreme skillful means and teaches the doctrine in accordance with reality for the benefit of sentient beings.
"I, the author of the treatise, shall speak" refers to the perfection of aspiration, as it indicates the desire to compose this treatise.
Regarding the Abhidharmakośa, its title is established as "Perfect," for it comprehensively subsumes seven meanings.
The verse says:
Wisdom, abandonment, and benefit for others, Expedient means, the aspiration, and the composition of the treatise.
The title *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma) should be understood as encompassing seven meanings.

Regarding these five categories of objects of knowledge—matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—the world at large lacks understanding; only the Buddha alone has realized them and eternally severed all afflictions.
Regarding "the most distant time," this refers to that which lies beyond three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past and future, which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know. How is this known?

In the past, there was a man who sought to go forth as a monk under Śāriputra; at that time, Śāriputra observed that this person lacked the roots of goodness for going forth over two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and thus did not grant his permission.

This person went to the Buddha seeking ordination; the World-Honored One observed him and saw that, though outside the Sangha, this man possessed some roots of goodness, and thus granted him permission to leave the household life.
He spoke in verse:
"The seeds of liberation in that person, as I observe them, are extremely subtle;
they are like pure gold hidden within various ores."
Maudgalyāyana observed his mother but could not discern where she had been reborn.
He went to ask the Buddha,
and the Buddha told him:
Your mother was born in the world-system of Mālinī, beyond three thousandfold world-systems.
Among such various kinds of distinctions, the wisdom of the śrāvakas and others does not comprehend them at all.

The fruits obtained through the cultivation of merit and wisdom are all for the benefit of others and not for self-interest; just as the pure moonlight shines upon the ten directions, so too is the compassionate vow of the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"The merit of dedicating [merit] and that which benefits oneself, The two merits of personal cultivation and dedication,
Are further caused by bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings."

The fruit of realization is not obtained from another but is attained by oneself; through the merit of one's conduct and vows as well as the merit of dedication, the benefit of both self and others is never in vain.
Thus, although it is said that self-benefit proceeds from cause and fruit, it is likewise able to benefit others.
A verse says:
Just as a wet nurse provides sweet food to nourish her child, Seeking his well-being and not her own;
So the Buddha cultivates merit and wisdom to attain Bodhi, Fundamentally to benefit sentient beings and not for himself.
The verse says:
Though the seasonal rain falls everywhere, Without seeds, sprouts do not grow;
Though the Buddha transforms the world, If conditions are lacking, fruition cannot be attained.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Who is a virtuous friend?
It is one who causes wisdom to arise through the Buddha’s teaching, and leads one away from negligence and unwholesome conduct; one who acts contrary to this is to be abandoned.

Regarding the Abhidharma, it should be understood as follows: innate wisdom serves as the cause for wisdom derived from hearing; wisdom derived from hearing serves as the cause for wisdom derived from reflection; wisdom derived from reflection serves as the cause for wisdom derived from cultivation; wisdom derived from cultivation serves as the cause for wisdom free from outflows; and wisdom free from outflows serves as the cause for Nirvana.
For this reason, it is called Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*), because it can increase the wisdom derived from hearing and so forth.
Alternatively, it is called "excellent" (*viśeṣa*) because it completely abandons all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and takes delight solely in nirvāṇa.
The truths of suffering, its origin, and the path serve as the wisdom for nirvāṇa; the Buddha’s teaching relies on the Dharma and not on the person.
The verse says:
Apart from the discernment of phenomena, there is truly no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions.
"Because of delusion, the world drifts in the ocean of existence; for this reason, the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
The treatise says:
"If one is apart from the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*), there is no superior means capable of extinguishing all delusions."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"While I am present, you should rely upon me; when I have entered parinirvāṇa, you will have no other basis for reliance.
You should rely upon the sūtras as your staff, so that you do not forget or lose them."
The Buddha said:
"For an elderly person to leave the household life and uphold my Tripiṭaka is extremely rare to find.
The Tripiṭaka consists of:"
First, the Sūtras; second, the Vinaya; third, the Miscellaneous Piṭaka.

Long ago, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who was intelligent and widely learned, possessing a thorough mastery of the Tripiṭaka. He once used his verbal karma to revile and insult renunciants and householders alike, comparing them to various birds and beasts such as owls, hooting owls, fish, and dogs.

After his life ended, as a result of this karmic retribution, he was born in the midst of the ocean, receiving the body of a great fish; its form was immense, possessing eighteen heads, and it underwent manifold sufferings.
Although the World-Honored One had appeared in the world, [the fish] was still not yet liberated.
Later, there were a thousand fishermen who, while laboriously catching fish, cast their net upon this fish; they dragged it out but could not pull it free.
Afterwards, several thousand people together dragged it out, seeing that it was of a different species, with many heads and a terrifying appearance.
The World-Honored One observed it and knew its life had reached its end; he then led the great assembly to the seashore, spread out his seat, and having sat down, called out to the fish, saying:
"Tripitaka!"
"Are you not the Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu from the time of a past Buddha?
Upon hearing this, the fish’s eyes filled with tears.
Then the World-Honored One explained its past causes for it; the fish felt remorse and ceased drinking and eating, whereupon it passed away and was reborn in the heavens.
At that time, the assembly who heard the Dharma each attained great benefit for their respective vehicles.
Since the five aggregates cannot encompass all phenomena, he did not rely upon the five aggregates to explain that there was first defilement and subsequently purification.
Because it purifies those defilements, the tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena are explained first, followed by the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
The verse says:
"The bhikṣu whose mind is tranquil Attains eternal cessation regarding all things."
Able to exhaust the limits of birth and death, One shall no longer undergo future existence.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle Two,
composed by the Venerable Sthiramati.
As it is said in a verse from the Treatise:
"The appearance of the Buddhas is bliss; The proclamation of the True Dharma is bliss;
The harmony of the Saṅgha is bliss; Practicing together with diligence is bliss."

The treatise states: In Uttarakuru, clothing weighs one *liang*; among the gods of the Four Great Kings, clothing weighs half a *liang*; in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, clothing weighs one *zhu*; in the Yāma Heaven, clothing weighs half a *zhu*; in the Tuṣita Heaven, clothing weighs one-quarter of a *zhu*; in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, clothing weighs one-eighth of a *zhu*; and in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, clothing weighs one-sixteenth of a *zhu*.
The above [concerns] the celestial garments of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), which cannot be weighed. If those garments in that realm were heavy, why say they cannot be weighed?
The garments worn by the various devas of the Form Realm correspond to the dimensions of their bodies; because they are as bright and pure as light, they cannot be described [in terms of weight].
The characteristics of manifest form shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"Whether the mind is distracted or absent, and whether it is pure or impure, it follows along with the stream."
The nature of being derived from the great elements (mahābhūta) is what is thereby called the unmanifest (avijñapti).
Regarding the six errors in the general exposition, the verse says:
"The first lacks continuity and is merely conventional; it is absent during mindless states, flows along [with the mind], and its characteristics are intermingled with the manifest."
Since terms such as "resetting" (pratisaṃdhāna) are not specified, it is therefore said that there are six errors here.
These refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they speak of all minds.
Among the six faults, this is explained because it contradicts one's own position.
The verse says:
"The act and so forth, other minds and so forth, as well as the unmanifest [karma] of the mindless state."
That which is non-obstructive and of a derivative nature is called non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Now, what is the difference between "earth" (*pṛthivī*) and the "earth element" (*pṛthivī-dhātu*)? The verse of the treatise says:
Earth refers to color and shape; It is a name established according to worldly convention.
The same applies to water and fire; wind and the elements are likewise so.
As it is said in the *Arthavargīya* of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*:
"Those who pursue various desires constantly give rise to longing."
If various desires are not fulfilled, they cause affliction and ruin, like being struck by an arrow.
Regarding the six consciousnesses, the verse of the treatise states:
Feeling has the nature of experiencing in accordance with contact; perception has the taking of images as its essence.

The remaining four [aggregates] are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Thus, these three beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), along with unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are termed the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
These consist of three aggregates and seven entities, as stated in a verse:
The three aggregates, unmanifest form, and the three types of unconditioned phenomena—these are subsumed within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana); the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is likewise.
The verse says:

Consciousness is the distinct discernment [of objects]; this is what is called the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), and it should be understood as the seven constituents (dhātus). When the six consciousnesses transform, they become the mind.
The verse says:
All phenomena are subsumed by the single aggregate, sense-field, and element;
they are subsumed by their own intrinsic nature and not by others, because they are devoid of the nature of another.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle Three.
The Venerable An-hui composed three categories:
first, the aggregate (*rāśi*); second, the gate of arising (*yoni*); and third, the genus (*nikāya*). "Aggregate" has the meaning of a heap. "Arising" has the meaning of a gate.
It refers to the sense that the mind and mental factors arise through a gate; for instance, visual consciousness arises with the eye as its gate.
This sūtra establishes six meanings regarding the gate of proof; however, as there are twelve mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), the sūtra states:

"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises, together with feeling, perception, and volition. This continues in the same manner up to: "With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three... [contact arises, together with feeling, perception, and volition].

The meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*). Just as a single mountain may contain many lineages of elements such as copper, iron, gold, and silver, which are called "many elements," so too, within a single body or a single continuum, there are eighteen types of lineages of phenomena, which are termed the "eighteen elements."
The eye-faculty is thus in the present, future, and past.
Regarding the inversion of ignorance, the verse says:
Like a fish dwelling in the mud, It leaps in the water, making it turbid.
In ignorance there is perverted perception; the same applies to defilement and affliction.
Regarding the designation "skandha," the verse says:
The Muni taught eighty thousand dharma-skandhas.
Its essence is either speech or names; this is necessarily subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The treatise verse says:
"The space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) refers to cavities and apertures; tradition states it is light and darkness."
The consciousness element consists of contaminated consciousness; it is the basis for the arising of sentient beings.
[From] Treatise, Volume 28: Among the eighteen elements, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
How many are resistant and how many are non-resistant?
How many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate?
The verse says:
One is visible, namely form; ten are material and possess resistance.
These eight, excluding visible form and sound, are acquired through non-informative [matter] and possess three types [of acquisition].
Five are non-discriminative, because they consist of investigative and recollective [discernment];
they have as their essence the distracted wisdom of the mental stage and all mindfulnesses of the mind.
The treatise states:
Regarding the explanation of discrimination (*vikalpa*), there are briefly three types:
first, discrimination by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*); second, conceptual discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*); and third, recollective discrimination (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
It is incorrect to say that there are eight kinds of discrimination because the five groups of sensory consciousness possess intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) but lack the other two.
They possess only intrinsic discrimination, and lack both constructive (*nirūpaṇa*) and recollective (*anusmaraṇa*) discrimination.
The sole conceptualization is called non-conceptualization.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle Four,
composed by the Venerable Sthiramati.
Regarding a single moment, the verse says:
The five internal [bases] possess the nature of being born of maturation and of accumulation; Sound lacks that which is born of maturation;
Eight [bases] are of the nature of outflow; And they also possess the nature of being born of maturation.
The remaining three [realities] are exclusively *dharmas*; the last three are exclusively momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
The five internal [bases] are the five elements (*dhātu*) of the eye and so forth.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are "seeing" (*darśana*) and how many are not?
The verse says:
The eye and a portion of the dharma-element are said to be the eight kinds of seeing;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not seeing, because it does not judge.
The eye sees visible forms when it is of the same class (*sabhāga*); it is not the consciousness that depends upon it which sees them.
It is traditionally taught that [the eye] cannot perceive obstructed visible forms.
The treatise says:
Because the eye is entirely seeing.
A portion of the dharma-dhātu—eight types—are seeing; the remainder are all not seeing.
Treatise:
Now, the definitive characteristics of these shall be briefly explained.
The verse says:
The eye is not inferior to the body; form and consciousness are not superior to the eye.
Visible forms are entirely [objects] of consciousness; the same applies to the two [types of sound] regarding the body.
As it is for the eye, so it is for the ear; the next three [senses] all belong to their own level.
Body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower one; it should be known that the mental faculty is not fixed.
Treatise:

Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), namely: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, faith faculty, vigor faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The commentary states: From which sūtra is this spoken?
It refers to a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who approached the Buddha, exchanged greetings with joy, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many faculties (*indriya*) are established to encompass all faculties exhaustively?
The Buddha said:
"I teach that twenty-two faculties encompass all faculties exhaustively."
If there is an objection to this and another faculty is proposed as a substitute, one should know that such a statement has words but no meaning.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā*, Fascicle Five,
composed by the Venerable Sthiramati.
Chapter Two: Analysis of the Faculties (Indriya-vibhāga), Part One.
Verse: It is traditionally taught that five [faculties] pertain to four [categories], while four faculties pertain to two kinds.
Among the five [faculties] and the eight [faculties] of defilement and purity, each acts as a predominant condition for its own respective sphere.
The treatise says:
This is because the five faculties, such as the eye, differ in their respective objects, from seeing forms up to hearing sounds.
The verse says:
Just as a person with clear vision can avoid present dangers,
so too those who are wise in this world can distance themselves from future suffering.
The learned are able to know the Dharma; The learned are able to leave behind transgressions;
The learned abandon what is meaningless; The learned attain *nirvāṇa*.
The verse says:
The body subsists through food; life depends upon food for its existence. Having eaten, the mind becomes joyful and at ease.
If a male enters the womb, he conceives love for the mother and hatred for the father.
If a female enters the womb, she conceives love for the father and hatred toward the mother;
from this it is known that the ability to link to a subsequent existence arises from a defiled mind.
Therefore, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is what links one to a subsequent existence.
The Sūtra says:
"When the semen and blood of the parents enter the womb, it is through being sustained by consciousness that they can achieve the state of kalala.
The commentary explains:
This reveals the meaning of how body and speech follow the mind.
As the Sūtra says:
"The mind leads the world; the mind thoroughly encompasses it. Thus, this single dharma that is the mind proceeds entirely according to its own power."
The verse says:
Because they exercise sovereignty over the cognition of their own respective objects, The six faculties are established in total.
From among the body, two faculties are established, Due to the sovereignty of female and male desire.
Regarding those who dwell together and those who dwell in a mixed manner, it should be known that for the increase of purity,
the five faculties— vitality and the [five] sensations— are established as faculties;
so too are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has fully known."
Regarding the attainment of successive paths, [the mind] is predominant over things such as nirvāṇa.
The treatise verse says:
"Physical displeasure is called suffering; that same [physical state], when pleasant, is called happiness."
And the mental joy of the three dhyānas; in other stages this is called *prīti*.
Mental displeasure is called *daurmanasya*; neutral equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the same in both cases.
Based on the nine stages—the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning—three faculties are established.
The verse says:
Only the final three are exclusively untainted; the material faculties, life, sorrow, and suffering are always known to be exclusively tainted; the remaining nine faculties pertain to both.
It is said that the final three faculties are necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*); apart from these three faculties, others do not extend to the untainted state.
As the Sūtra says:
"At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained perfect enlightenment, he reflected thus:"

The Dharma realized by me is profound and subtle, difficult to see and difficult to understand, inconceivable, beyond the sphere of discursive thought, known only by the wise, and inaccessible to the foolish and ignorant.
These sentient beings have long practiced false teachings and are attached to the various realms of existence; because they are deluded and distracted by various views, they are unable to understand.
Because they do not understand, they are unable to believe and accept [the teaching], and instead give rise to affliction and distress.
"What I have spoken has been of no benefit; my labors have been in vain.
It would be better to abide in the Dharma of tranquility and experience the bliss of liberation.
Having formed this thought, he remained silent.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had formed such a thought, reflected to himself:
"The sentient beings in this world have suffered much ruin and destruction."

Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, having realized the unsurpassed Dharma—profound, vast, subtle, and wondrous—considered that sentient beings might be unable to believe and accept it; he therefore dwelt in secluded tranquility, experiencing the bliss of the present life.
"I should go to him and entreat the World-Honored One to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
Having formed this thought, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Brahma palace and arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times, they withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The sentient beings in this world have long practiced divergent teachings; entangled by the delusions of views, they transmigrate through birth and death, having no refuge and no protector."

The World-Honored One has practiced the bodhisattva path for kalpas beyond measure on behalf of all sentient beings; having now attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment and realized the unsurpassed Dharma, he has appeared in the world like the udumbara flower.
He does not preach to sentient beings according to their capacities, but dwells in secluded silence.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will descend with great compassion, take pity on the world, and expound the essentials of the True Dharma for all sentient beings.

There are sentient beings whose various fetters are thin and slight, whose capacities have matured, and who, being of sharp faculties, are easily transformed; yet because they have not heard the Dharma, their [virtues] naturally diminish and they lose the great benefit of the Dharma.

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will open the gate of ambrosia for all sentient beings and preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, so that all living beings may obtain benefit, peace, and happiness.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King exhorted the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:

"The World-Honored One appears as a rare Udumbara flower; Difficult to encounter throughout vast eons, you are met but once now. I pray you preach the supreme Dharma, To deliver all beings from suffering."
"May all sentient beings universally obtain the benefit of the Dharma; I only pray that you shall widely open the gate of the Deathless Nectar.

At that time, having heard the verse of exhortation from the Brahmā King, the World-Honored One gave rise to great compassion and, with his eye of the Way, observed all sentient beings: some had dull faculties and were attached to various states of existence; some had middling faculties and felt slight weariness toward birth and death; and some had sharp faculties and were not negligent.

In this way, the World-Honored One observes all sentient beings in the world as they dwell, whether being born or growing up; their faculties are either sharp or dull, and some are easily transformed and attain the Way.
Having known this as it truly is, he accepted the invitation of the Great Brahmā King and consented to turn the wheel of Dharma, speaking these verses:
"Great Brahmā King, listen well and attentively: The Dharma I have attained is most subtle and profound.
I shall now expound it extensively for your sake, So that you may obtain peace and happiness throughout the long night."
The verse says:
Life is exclusively maturation; sorrow and the final eight are not.
The [five] material faculties, the mind, and the remaining four sensations—each of these may be of both types.
Treatise:
The life-faculty alone is necessarily maturation (*vipāka*).
Commentary:
There is not a single life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
The verse says:
The Northern Continent has a fixed lifespan of a thousand years; In the Western and Eastern continents, it decreases by half a day [each].
The lifespan in this continent is indefinite; at the end it is ten years, while at the beginning it is immeasurable.
May all other sentient beings of the world, through their remaining meritorious karma, likewise make this aspiration:
"May we be long-lived."
Nor does one wish to say:
"May I live for a hundred years, or for ninety, eighty, or seventy years.
Or perhaps there are honored persons, relatives, friends, and others who constantly offer this blessing:
"May you live long.
Nor does one state a fixed duration, such as "for this many years," and so forth;
rather, people of this continent make this aspiration while performing various deeds accompanied by a mind of attachment.
The Sūtra states:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, the human lifespan was eighty thousand years; and so on, until the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years."
I have now appeared in the world when the human lifespan is one hundred years,
with few exceeding it and many falling short.
If the lifespan were not subject to such fixed limits, why did the World-Honored One speak in this way?
At the beginning of the kalpa, the sense faculties and the primary elements were superior, and thus lifespans were extended.
Now, as these have gradually deteriorated, it is difficult for a lifespan to reach even ten years.
When one's merit is exhausted, death occurs; it is not due to the end of one's allotted life-span.
Restoring old stupas and temples can prolong one’s lifespan.
The verse says:
The holy life is perfectly established, The noble path has been well cultivated.
When life comes to an end, one rejoices, as if casting off a multitude of ailments.
